title: Ἔριφος καὶ λύκος ⟨αὐλῶν⟩
titleEn: The Kid and the Piping Wolf
part: The Kid and the Piping Wolf (Chambry 107 · Perry 97)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 107 (= Perry 97). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔριφος ὑστερήσας ἀπὸ ποίμνης ὑπὸ λύκου κατεδιώκετο· ἐπιστραφεὶς δὲ ὁ ἔριφος λέγει τῷ λύκῳ· « Πέπεισμαι, λύκε, ὅτι σὸν βρῶμά εἰμι· ἀλλ’ ἵνα μὴ ἀδόξως ἀποθάνω, αὔλησον, ὅπως ὀρχήσωμαι. »
sentences.tr: Eriphos hysterēsas apo poimnēs hypo lykou katediōketo· epistrapheis de ho eriphos legei tōi lykōi· « Pepeismai, lyke, hoti son brōma eimi· all’ hina mē adoxōs apothanō, aulēson, hopōs orchēsōmai. »
sentences.l: A kid, having fallen behind the flock, was being chased down by a wolf; and turning round the kid says to the wolf: « I am persuaded, wolf, that I am your food; but so that I may not die without glory, pipe, that I may dance. »
sentences.i: A kid that had fallen behind the flock was being run down by a wolf; and the kid turned and said to the wolf: « I am quite sure, wolf, that I am your dinner; but so that I may not die inglorious, pipe for me, that I may dance. »
sentences.n: λέγει is the historic present — the narrative slips into the present tense at the moment of speech, and the literal line keeps it. πέπεισμαι is the perfect middle-passive of πείθω, 'I have been persuaded', hence simply 'I am convinced'. The αὐλός is the double reed-pipe, closer to an oboe than to a flute; αὔλησον is its aorist imperative. ὅπως with the subjunctive here is a purpose clause, like the ἵνα just before it.

sentences.t: Αὐλοῦντος δὲ τοῦ λύκου καὶ ὀρχουμένου τοῦ ἐρίφου, οἱ κύνες ἀκούσαντες καὶ ἐξελθόντες κατεδίωκον τὸν λύκον.
sentences.tr: Aulountos de tou lykou kai orchoumenou tou eriphou, hoi kynes akousantes kai exelthontes katediōkon ton lykon.
sentences.l: And the wolf piping and the kid dancing, the dogs, having heard and having come out, began to chase the wolf.
sentences.i: And while the wolf piped and the kid danced, the dogs heard, came out and gave chase to the wolf.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes side by side: a noun and its participle set in the genitive, standing free of the main clause's grammar and giving the circumstances — 'while the wolf piped and the kid danced'. κατεδίωκον is imperfect: the chase is under way, not finished.

sentences.t: Ἐπιστραφεὶς δὲ ὁ λύκος λέγει τῷ ἐρίφῳ· « Ταῦτα ἐμοὶ καλῶς γίνεται· ἔδει γάρ με μακελλάριον ὄντα αὐλητὴν μὴ μιμεῖσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Epistrapheis de ho lykos legei tōi eriphōi· « Tauta emoi kalōs ginetai· edei gar me makellarion onta aulētēn mē mimeisthai. »
sentences.l: And the wolf, turning round, says to the kid: « These things happen to me rightly; for I, being a butcher, ought not to have imitated a piper. »
sentences.i: And the wolf turned and said to the kid: « This serves me right; being a butcher, I had no business playing the piper. »
sentences.n: ἔδει with a plain infinitive and no ἄν states what ought to have been done and was not — 'I ought not to have imitated'. μακελλάριος is the butcher of the meat-market, a word taken over from Latin macellarius; it is late Greek, and one of the seams where the collection's long transmission shows.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ παρὰ γνώμην τοῦ καιροῦ τι πράττοντες καὶ ὧν ἐν χερσὶν ἔχουσιν ὑστεροῦνται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi para gnōmēn tou kairou ti prattontes kai hōn en chersin echousin hysterountai.
sentences.l: Thus those who do anything contrary to the judgement of the occasion fall short even of what they have in their hands.
sentences.i: So it is that those who act against what the moment advises lose even what they already hold.
sentences.n: ὧν is a relative attracted into the genitive of its unexpressed antecedent (τούτων ἃ … ἔχουσιν becomes ὧν … ἔχουσιν); ὑστεροῦνται then takes that genitive, since one falls short of a thing. The word answers the ὑστερήσας of the first line: the kid who lagged behind the flock leaves the wolf lagging behind his dinner.
